chunks: "A latch is level-sensitive: while its enable, or clock, is at the active level, the output follows the input, so it's transparent.
When the enable goes inactive, it holds the last value.
A flip-flop is edge-triggered: it only looks at its input at the instant of the clock edge, say the rising edge, copies it to the output, and ignores changes everywhere else.
The relationship is that a D flip-flop is built from two D latches in series with opposite clock phases, called master and slave.
While the clock is low, the master is transparent and the slave holds.
At the rising edge the master closes and the slave opens, so the output updates once, with whatever the master held. Why does it matter?
Flip-flops make timing simple: data moves exactly one stage per clock, so you just check setup and hold at each edge.
Latches pass glitches through when they're transparent and the timing depends on when data arrives within the open window.
The upside is that latches are smaller and faster, and allow time borrowing between stages, so they show up in clock-gating cells and custom high-speed designs.
A classic gotcha is that incomplete if statements in RTL infer latches by accident."
